Olive growers on edge due to extreme heat: “Around 25% of olives will not be suitable for table olive production”
Francisco Manuel Fernández Pérez, COAG representative, warned during the VIII BusinessAGRO Tertulia about the consequences of heatwaves in the final stretch of summer.
Last Thursday, September 3, the VIII BusinessAGRO Olive Grove Tertulia was held in La Puebla de Cazalla (Seville), a forum where producers and cooperatives expressed their concern about the impact of the extreme heat of recent days in Andalusia on olive groves and, consequently, the uncertainty it is creating regarding yield forecasts for the upcoming season.
During the roundtable that closed the event, Francisco Manuel Fernández Pérez, national table olive representative of COAG, said he had been feeling “uneasy” for several days because temperatures above 40ºC in recent days will have a direct impact on his olive trees.
“As of today, after these days of intense heat, we have confirmed that around 25% of olives will not be suitable for table olive production. They no longer have the size they should,” he warned at the Oleand Manzanilla Olive headquarters.
The direct consequence is that producers, in these cases, have no choice but to divert these olives to the mills in an attempt to extract whatever olive oil they can. And they must resign themselves to giving up table olive production, which commands a higher market price.
Along these lines, Ángel Abellán Hernández, export manager at Oleand Manzanilla Olive, called for caution with forecasts, noting that “if temperatures persist for another week, the yield estimate will likely drop.” He also recalled that the most accurate yield figures are those published in November.
Use of yield forecasts to push prices down
On this issue, participants also highlighted a side effect of publishing table olive and olive oil harvest forecasts when there is still not enough information available.
Gabriel Cabello López, president of Cooperativas Agro‑alimentarias de Sevilla, pointed out that buyers of olive growers take advantage of these early forecasts to lower prices and pay farmers less, even though the figures are not yet confirmed.
“Forecasts help us understand the potential of the trees, but they are not confirmed data,” he concluded.
